newsitem.title: UK: Holiday-bound Britons dizzy as sterling soars.
newsitem.headline: Holiday-bound Britons dizzy as sterling soars.

text.p: Sun, sea and surf aside, the pound will buy British holiday-makers more champagne in France, beer in Germany, ouzo in Greece and chianti in Italy this summer as it cruises multi-year peaks against European currencies.
Against the lira, for instance, the pound rocketed this week to its highest level since 1969.
"Money is going much further...The more you are planning to spend overseas, the better value you'll get," said Jackie Gibson, spokeswoman at the Association of British Travel Agents.
Against muscular currencies like the German mark and French franc the pound has soared nearly 30 percent from last July to 2.9758 marks and above 10.00 francs this week, its highest since 1991.
Some 13.7 million Britons are expected to travel overseas this year, with France attracting the largest number, if weekend breaks and day trips are included.
For longer holidays the allure of Spain's Costa del Sol will attract the brunt of Britons -- with four out of 10 holiday-makers landing there for a break.
"As far as the holiday cost goes, Spain remains way ahead of the others...There are so many tour operators and the competition is fierce," said ABTA's Gibson.

The pound, fuelled by a booming economy and an attractively high yield compared to its European counterparts, has swelled against the currencies of the so-called "Club Med" countries of Spain, Greece, Portugal and Italy.

Against the Spanish peseta, it has jumped more than 25 percent from last summer to over 251.00 pesetas this week, hitting peaks last scaled in 1971. And one pound is now equivalent to 300.00 Portuguese escudos after a climb of some 24 percent since last July.
In some cases the pound has hit dizzying heights not seen in two decades or more.
It has raced some 27 percent against the Greek drachma since last summer, for instance, to 20-year highs around 468.5624.
Against the lira it is at its highest level since 1969, although with a rise of nearly 13 percent to 2906.40 lire since last July the gains are not as heady compared to the other Club Med currencies.

For holiday goers, buying power has been compounded by the pound's strength and stable inflation across the continent, as countries racing to meet the criteria for joining Europe's single currency in 1999 kept their inflation in check.

"Gains around 25 percent are tremendous...And sterling's value is even better as inflation across most of Europe remains steady...," said Fred Tilly, senior foreign exchange trader at Thomas Cook, a UK travel agent and tour operator accounting for some 12-14 percent of market share.
One pound, for instance, will buy nearly two bottles of beer in Portugal while 65 pence will buy one on Spain's Costa Del Sol, with a three-course meal costing as little as 8.80 pounds.

For long-haul travel, dollar-linked currencies are also good value against sterling since the pound has gained on the U.S. currency as well. Against the dollar, the pound jumped to a near six-month high of $1.6956 this week.
"Dollar-linked currencies are the big ones -- basically, your money can go further. Dominican Republic is the big story for long-haul, followed by Florida," said Thomsons' spokeswoman.

With bad weather in Britain -- June was one of the wettest months on record -- bigger spending power in consumer hands after building society windfall payments and sterling's strength, Britons are champing at the bit to flee overseas.

"After the share allocations and the rain, we saw business increase some 15 percent on the week. And our total figure for June shows a rise of around 30 percent" said Richard Grummitt, public relations manager at Thomas Cook.
"Our foreign exchange sales through June have been really, really strong," he added.
With the mighty pound expected to remain strong as UK interest rates rise, industry sources see few clouds on the horizon for British holiday makers.
"The only downside, from the British Tourist Authority point of view, is that it makes Britain less competitive to our European neighbours," said ABTA's Gibson.
"It is good news for our holiday makers but not such good news for the industry here," she said.
